chapter: Benny Goodman and the big band
title: Leaving school for Goodman, freelancing, and the 1979 Bird and Prez tribute concert
summary: Playing in many bands, then the 1979 concert tribute with Howard McGhee, Dickie Wells and others.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: You’ve got to have a doctorate to do anything. But anyway, I left school and went to work for Benny Goodman. And he was paying me I think it was $250 a week to come in and my job was to say — you know to have a stack of arrangements and you would say now there’s three versions of the “King Porter Stomp” here. Now one’s in — two are in D flat, there’s one in G, and this one has Fletcher Henderson’s name on it but this one doesn’t but it says Ziggy on the trumpet part or something like that. And so I mean it was just a dream come true. That lasted, I forget how long, a few months. And I wrote this little thing and the music went to the New York Public Library and that was it. So in New York at that time I mean this is 1980, and already you know I could make a living, I mean, playing in just a million different bands, you know what it was like, you know, Stan Rubin’s band one night and then filling in at Eddie Condon’s maybe one night and then a wedding that paid more money than all of it put together, a bar mitzvah then, playing solo piano in a restaurant and then playing with a million different bands, you know for cheap money. But it all added up and I was 21, 22 years old, what the hell you know. So that was the end of that. Now I had done my first concert, again with my family, my parents put up the money for it, although it did turn a profit, and in June 1979 I guess I was just about to turn 21, I produced a concert at Carnegie Recital Hall and it was called “A Tribute to Bird and Prez.” And we played the Super Sax arrangements and then I orchestrated these Lester Young solos for a sax section and myself. And the featured soloists were Howard McGhee, who I had already been working with a little bit, Warren Vache, Eddie Bert, Dickie Wells, Joe Albany, I was already in his quartet. Joe Albany on piano. He had just come back to New York and was healthy for a short time, Herb Ellis, a bass player I was working with named Peck Morrison who was in the Duke Ellington band, and Mel Lewis, who I’d started a friendship with on drums. So that was June 1979. We got reviewed in the New York Times, you know, which was not a bad review by John S. Wilson. So I was kind of building up, you know, starting to have a chance to do some of this stuff. Then when I stopped working for Benny I just went back to playing and whatever, but when I was going through his big band music in the course of working on this thing, I asked him if I could copy a few arrangements. I really didn’t know why I was going to copy them. Well I think I might have had an inkling. And so he let me copy some music on the Xerox machine, just, I don’t know, five or six arrangements.
